description: Registry of Sufyan Ahmad's DevOps engineering projects. Rendered by index.html (#lab) and used to keep every new project distinct from the existing ones.

projects.name: SLO-Driven Progressive Delivery with Automated Rollback
projects.summary: When a team releases a new version of an app, this system first gives it to only a few users and checks if it works well. If it does, more users get it step by step. If it doesn't, the system automatically switches everyone back to the old version.
projects.problem: Usually a new version goes to all users at once. If it has a bug, everyone is affected, and someone has to notice it and undo it by hand, often in the middle of the night.
projects.engineering_problem: Release safety: gate production rollouts on SLO/error-budget signals and roll back automatically.
projects.architecture: Argo Rollouts canary with background AnalysisTemplate querying Prometheus per pod-template hash; multi-window burn-rate alerts; Grafana provisioned as code; kind-based e2e in GitHub Actions.
projects.unique_capability: SLIs/SLOs, error budgets, multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting, progressive delivery with automated rollback, fail-safe analysis.
projects.tagline: New app versions are tested on a few users first and undone automatically if something breaks.
projects.benefit: Bad releases reach only a few users for less than a minute and are undone automatically, so teams can release often without fear, and nobody has to watch every release.
projects.simple_name: Safe app releases that undo themselves

projects.name: Automated Linux Server Hardening & Monitoring with Ansible
projects.simple_name: One command that locks down a new server
projects.summary: You run one command and a brand-new Linux server is made safe: only people with the right key can log in, unwanted connections are blocked, attackers who keep guessing passwords are blocked automatically, and security updates install by themselves. A dashboard then keeps watching every server.
projects.problem: A new server is quite open by default and bots start guessing passwords within minutes. Securing it by hand takes long, every server ends up a bit different, and nobody notices when someone later switches a protection off.
projects.benefit: Every server gets exactly the same protection in a few minutes, its security score is measured (61 → 77 in the lab), and running the same command again shows and fixes anything that was changed by hand.
projects.tagline: One command makes a new Linux server secure, and a dashboard keeps checking that it stays that way.
projects.engineering_problem: Configuration drift and inconsistent manual hardening of Linux servers.
projects.architecture: Nine idempotent Ansible roles with validate-before-write (sshd -t, nft -c, visudo) and lockout guards; Molecule on Ubuntu 24.04/Debian 12/Debian 13; Docker lab with real SSH, attacker and Prometheus/Grafana; check/diff drift detection; Lynis score exported via the node_exporter textfile collector.
projects.unique_capability: Safe, repeatable server hardening with measured before/after security scores, drift detection and monitoring of the protections themselves.

projects.name: PostgreSQL Backups You Can Trust: Restore Drills & Point-in-Time Recovery
projects.simple_name: Database backups that are tested every night
projects.summary: Every change in the database is copied to safe, encrypted storage within a minute. Every night the system practises a restore on a spare copy and checks that nothing is missing, like a fire drill. If someone deletes data by mistake, one command brings the database back to the second before it happened.
projects.problem: Many teams have backups but never try to restore them. On the day they really need them, they discover the backups are broken, too old, or that nobody knows the password, and the data is gone.
projects.benefit: You know every morning that the backups really work, how long a restore takes (6 seconds in the lab) and how much data could be lost (under a minute). An alert appears long before the backups are needed.
projects.tagline: Backups are restored and checked automatically every night, so you know they work before you need them.
projects.engineering_problem: Untested backups: unknown restorability, RTO and RPO; no point-in-time recovery.
projects.architecture: PostgreSQL 18 archives WAL through a dedicated pgBackRest repo host (mutual TLS) into encrypted S3; full/diff/incremental backups, daily verify and an automatic restore drill with amcheck; isolated networks; Pushgateway + Prometheus alerts; point-in-time and lost-volume recovery scripts.
projects.unique_capability: Proves restorability every day with measured RTO/RPO, and is tested against an accidental DROP TABLE, a lost database disk, a storage outage, bit rot and a lost encryption key.

projects.name: Zero-Trust Software Supply Chain for Kubernetes: Signed Builds, SBOMs & Admission Control
projects.simple_name: Only code we built ourselves can run in production
projects.summary: Every app our pipeline builds gets a digital seal and three signed papers: where it came from, a security scan, and a list of everything inside. A guard at the door of the cluster checks the seal and the papers before anything starts. No seal from our pipeline, no entry.
projects.problem: Most clusters run any app that sits in the company's image store. If an attacker steals that store's password, slips a bad step into the build, or changes one line in git, their code runs in production and nobody notices.
projects.benefit: A stolen password or a sneaky git change is no longer enough to run code in production. Each release is attacked automatically before it ships, and an alert appears when something is blocked or when an app already running turns out to have a serious security hole.
projects.tagline: Production only runs apps that carry our pipeline's seal, so a stolen password is not enough to get in.
projects.engineering_problem: Clusters trust registry contents and git, not proof of origin; CI pipelines themselves are attack paths.
projects.architecture: GitHub Actions builds a distroless Go image, gates on Trivy, pushes by digest and signs keylessly with cosign (OIDC, Fulcio, Rekor) plus SLSA provenance, vulnerability and SBOM attestations; an e2e attack test runs on a fresh kind cluster before the digest is promoted to git; Argo CD deploys; Kyverno CEL policies verify the release identity, provenance, scan and SBOM at admission; Trivy Operator and Prometheus watch what runs.
projects.unique_capability: Refuses images signed by a different workflow of the same repository (injected-workflow attacks), tampered and unsigned images, and malicious GitOps commits, and proves it on every release.
